analysis.one_liner: Removes marijuana from federal criminal drug laws, erases past federal cannabis convictions, and taxes legal sales to fund communities hurt by enforcement.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 220-204 on April 1, 2022, but the Senate never voted on it, so federal marijuana prohibition stayed on the books.
analysis.plain_summary: The MORE Act would have taken marijuana off the federal list of illegal drugs, wiping out federal criminal penalties for growing, selling, or possessing it. It would have set up a process to erase past federal cannabis convictions, stopped deportations and benefits denials based on marijuana offenses, and created programs—paid for by a new tax on legal cannabis sales—to help communities hurt most by decades of drug enforcement. The House passed it, but the Senate never voted, so the law did not change.
analysis.who_benefits: People with federal cannabis convictions, whose records could be expunged; non-citizens who faced deportation for cannabis offenses; people currently facing federal marijuana prosecution; communities of color targeted by decades of unequal enforcement, who would receive job training, reentry services, and legal aid funded by a new federal cannabis tax; and small cannabis businesses that would gain access to Small Business Administration services [S2][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with cannabis convictions and hard-hit communities

how_it_helps.text: Removes marijuana from the Controlled Substances Act, eliminating federal criminal penalties for manufacturing, distributing, and possessing cannabis.
Establishes a process to expunge federal cannabis convictions and conduct sentencing review hearings, and makes the change retroactive to past cases and convictions.
Ends deportation and denial of federal public benefits and immigration protections based on cannabis conduct or convictions.

Creates an Opportunity Trust Fund, funded by a new federal cannabis excise tax, to pay for job training, reentry services, legal aid for expungement, and substance-use services in communities harmed by the war on drugs.
Makes Small Business Administration loans and services available to cannabis-related businesses, and funds programs to help people arrested or convicted of cannabis offenses enter the legal industry.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of cannabis products, who would pay a new federal excise tax starting at 5% and an annual $1,000-per-location occupational tax — costs likely passed to consumers in legal markets. Taxpayers currently bear about $3.6 billion a year enforcing prohibition, which the bill would redirect [S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Cannabis businesses through new federal taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new federal excise tax on cannabis products (starting at 5% of price, rising to 8%) plus a $1,000 annual occupational tax on producers, which would raise prices for consumers and burden small producers even as it funds reinvestment programs.

The bill preserves federal workplace drug-testing authority and transportation regulators' power to screen for marijuana use, so some federal employees and safety-sensitive workers would still face penalties for cannabis use.

Critics of legalization generally warn that wider commercial availability raises youth access and impaired-driving risks; the bill directs NHTSA, NIOSH, and the Department of Education to study those impacts rather than resolve them in advance [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to individuals with records, to people facing deportation, and to communities of color targeted by enforcement are large and hard to dispute; ending 600,000 arrests a year saves both people and taxpayer money [S5]. The real drawbacks are design ones: the bill imposes a high federal excise tax on cannabis products that would likely keep prices elevated and preserve a black-market undercut, and its reinvestment programs depend on administration and eligibility rules working as intended. The tax burden on the emerging industry is the strongest good-faith objection, even from supporters of legalization itself.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed the bill in April 2022, but the Senate sent it to its Finance Committee and never voted on it before the two-year Congress ended, killing the bill.

narrative.text: On April 1, 2022, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit 202-220 and then passed the MORE Act 220-204, with 217 of 220 Democrats voting yes and only 3 of 209 Republicans.
On April 4, 2022, the Senate received the bill and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where it remained with no further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023.

The bill would have removed marijuana from the Controlled Substances Act, established an expungement process for federal cannabis convictions, and created a trust fund for communities impacted by the war on drugs.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal cannabis enforcement continued unchanged: prosecutors, and the existing arrest, conviction, and deportation machinery kept operating, and the emerging legal cannabis industry remained cut off from federal banking and small-business support.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal enforcement status quo; no one new

for.name: Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and led it through the Judiciary Committee, which reported it 26-15.

for.name: 217 of 220 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for passage, supplying nearly all of the bill's 220 votes.

for.name: 3 of 209 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Crossed party lines to vote for passage.

against.name: 202 of 209 Senate-eligible Republicans (as reflected in the House vote of 202 Republicans)
against.what_they_did: Nearly unanimously opposed the bill in the House, voting for the motion to recommit and against final passage.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 4, 2022, and never reported it out; no Senate vote ever occurred.

against.name: 202 of 209 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted 202-7 against passage and unanimously for the motion to recommit designed to sink the bill.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, 217 of 220 Democrats voted for the bill while 202 of 209 Republicans voted against it; the bill then died without any Senate action.

industries.note: Descheduling would remove federal criminal penalties and let cannabis businesses access SBA loans, banking-adjacent services, and normal tax treatment, while subjecting them to a new federal excise tax of 5-8% plus licensing and bonding rules.

industries.industry: Criminal justice and enforcement apparatus (prosecutors, private prisons, drug testing contractors)
industries.note: The bill eliminates over 600,000 annual arrests for possession and removes cannabis offenses as a basis for deportation, shrinking the caseload that enforcement of prohibition generates.
The bill never became law, so cheaper legal cannabis could not compete with them; its death preserved the status quo in which legal cannabis is barred from ordinary federal business channels.
